title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent to device configuration is a core NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as intent→configuration translators that can accelerate operations, but probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, and unsafe commands. Recent literature advocates hybrid patterns that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops as operational floor‑safety nets. However, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics are limited. We implement and preregister a narrowly scoped paired experiment to evaluate the operational effect of a minimal guarded pipeline composed of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator performing canonicalization and rule/dependency checks, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator reports violations. The core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions are (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts, (ii) confirmatory statistics derived from those artifacts, (iii) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied to the observed contingency counts, and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Work applying LLMs to network configuration and intent translation has grown rapidly. Recent system demonstrations show promising intent→configuration synthesis in lab settings but also document failure modes—misordering, omission, and overconfidence—that affect operational safety [1]. Parallel work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) shows that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating similar guarded architectures for NetOps [2],[3]. Classic deterministic network verification (Minesweeper/Batfish, header‑space analysis) provides algorithmic foundations for validators that can statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [4]. Surveys and standards work emphasize generate→verify→repair patterns and highlight auditability and human‑oversight concerns as open challenges for production NetOps adopters [5]. Our study positions itself at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired evaluation that directly measures first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor‑guardrail.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) before observing final outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. Design and sampling: Paired within‑task design with a fixed deterministic seed list of 300 tasks produced by a frozen task generator; each seed yields a single shared initial LLM candidate that serves as the baseline response and the starting point for guarded validation/repair. Planned episodes = 600; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Model and provider settings: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini and the execution manifest records the archived model configuration (execution/model_configuration.json). That archived model configuration records "temperature": null; a null/unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling (temperature=0) and therefore sampling determinism was unspecified for the run — an operational caveat that can affect generator variance and thus inferential interpretation. Validator and scoring semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized responses to a normalized AST and applied explicit workflow and dependency checks (full intent‑constraint validation). The validator trace fields (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, valid flag) determined repair invocation. Repair adapter: Invoked only when the validator reported violations on the shared candidate; restricted to a single automated repair attempt per episode; repaired outputs were revalidated by the same deterministic validator. Contamination and exclusions: Deterministic AST equality and near‑duplicate lexical thresholds were preregistered; any exact duplicates would trigger deterministic exclusion and replacement from a reserve set. Primary estimand and analysis: Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Preregistered primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05); paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) were preregistered. Missingness/retry policy: provider/infrastructure failures handled with a single retry; primary missingness treatment drops pairs only if both calls failed. All artifacts, seeds, scoring rules, and analysis code were archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic exclusions for contamination were required. Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.00. Absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The single discordant pair is pair-000229 (baseline failed; guarded succeeded after repair); this episode and its validator/repair trace are archived in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded interpretation: The observed contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) constrains inferential outcomes: with only one discordant pair the maximum resolvable absolute paired improvement is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333, explaining why the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction (planned against an assumed baseline of 0.40) could not be detected. The shared_initial_candidate pairing was chosen for ecological validity but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces informative discordant counts; power planning must account for this tradeoff. Repair effectiveness is a conditional estimand (P(repair succeeds | initial failure)); observing 1/1 yields point estimate 100% but with a wide CI, underscoring the need to design for an adequate number of initial failures when repair success is a primary claim. Construct validity: our validator performs static deterministic checks (canonicalization and intent constraints) rather than dynamic emulation; runtime semantics (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability) remain unmeasured and require emulation to assess. Diagnostics: structured validator traces (violation_codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count) proved essential for failure‑mode analysis and for the reproducible repair that corrected pair-000229. Design recommendations: (1) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to ensure a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence or a preregistered discordant‑pair target; (2) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and include those choices in power calculations; (3) include emulation when runtime semantic claims are intended. These recommendations are traceable to artifacts archived in the execution manifest.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline generation yielded 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline yielded 300/300 valid outputs; the single automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures or target discordant counts, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (c) include emulation to measure runtime semantic effects when deployment claims are intended. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
